title: The roles of three enterprise apps and APIs

opening.headline: When each department uses its own AI tools, distinguish between what enterprise apps and APIs are responsible for and establish a corporate-standard foundation.
body: The legal team subscribes to chat-based apps on a team basis, the development team receives model API keys and integrates them into internal tools, and the sales team often uses external services via personal accounts. While each team has its own rationale for these choices, a common issue arises in that it's not visible in one place who is entering what data into which tools.

In this course, we examine the control capabilities provided to administrators by three enterprise applications: ChatGPT Enterprise, Claude Enterprise, and Gemini Enterprise. We then compare the differences between SSO, which determines the login method, and SCIM, which manages account creation and deletion, and explore who is responsible for designing control frameworks when building directly via API. Finally, we analyze a case where legal and development teams have differing requirements and confirm how to consolidate these two domains into a single responsibility matrix.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the roles of ChatGPT Enterprise, Claude Enterprise, Gemini Enterprise and API construction
It is possible to distinguish the control scope that a team must directly design when building management features and APIs for enterprise applications.

screens.title: Each department uses different tools and there are no company-wide standards.
screens.lead: First, let's examine a common scenario within an organization. Consider four departments reading how AI is being used and think about what's missing.

paragraphs: Let's examine how AI is being used across different departments within an organization. The legal team subscribes to a chat-based app at the team level for summarizing contracts. The development team obtained a model API key and integrated it directly into internal tools. The sales team uses external AI services via personal accounts to refine proposal content.

All three teams made reasonable choices, but as a whole organization, we cannot answer several key questions. We have no centralized way to verify who is putting what data into which tools, whether former employees' accounts have been properly cleaned up across all tools, or which features are permitted in each tool.

To solve this issue, it's first necessary to distinguish between two major approaches to using AI. One approach involves deploying enterprise-grade apps that come with a management console, while the other involves building custom services by calling model APIs. These two approaches differ in where responsibility for control is placed.
The only question to be answered in this class is: What responsibilities does building enterprise apps and APIs each have?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: AI services used for personal accounts do not fall into either of the two categories mentioned above. Please pay close attention to areas where management visibility is lost.

screens.outro: Now let us imagine what your organization looks like.

screens.title: Think back on how our organization uses AI.
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: How can AI be used within our organization?
items.answer: Most organizations are divided into three main categories: subscription apps used by employees after logging in, custom services built by developers through API calls, and individual, self-managed usage methods. The first two categories fall within areas that administrators can control via settings, while the third remains outside of administrative control. This course covers the first two categories.

items.prompt: In a team using a subscription-based app, who creates and who removes accounts?
items.answer: Administrators invite members or create accounts by integrating with an identity provider and then clean up accounts when employees resign or move. Manually performing this process is prone to omissions. Therefore, the Business App provides separate features for SSO, which defines the login method, and provisioning, which automatically aligns accounts. We'll examine the differences between these two features in detail later.

items.prompt: Did any management interface exist for tools developed using an API?
items.answer: Tools created by directly calling APIs are not automatically managed by the admin console. Designing prompts, tool connections, logging, and permissions falls squarely on the team's responsibility. Unlike enterprise apps, the greater flexibility comes at the cost of having to manually implement control.

screens.outro: First, let's examine the management features of enterprise apps configured by administrators.

screens.title: Three enterprise apps: what the administrator controls
screens.lead: Select each tab to verify the control options available to administrators for the three products. The common features of the three products are summarized in the last tab.

visual.alt: This is a diagram showing three enterprise apps all built upon the same common structure of workspace-level management.
labels: Workspace-level management: members, seats, feature access, apps, analytics

tabs.label: ChatGPT Enterprise
tabs.body:
The center of management is Workspace settings. Workspace owners and administrators configure members, seat defaults, feature access, GPT governance, apps, analytics, and identity control within this area. Simply select the profile icon to open Workspace settings.

Another axis is custom roles. Using role-based access control (RBAC), functionality access permissions can be bundled into reusable units and assigned to members or groups. Since the same settings do not need to be repeated for each individual, this becomes increasingly effective as the organization grows. Plugin and marketplace management is handled separately in the Admin Console.

tabs.label: Claude Enterprise
tabs.body:
The administrator area includes roles, seats, and groups, and also covers group-specific spending limits, custom roles, and plugin management. A key feature is the ability to manage departments based on usage volume by setting separate limits for large and small departments.

The method for onboarding users is determined in the Organization Settings under User Provisioning. By default, invitations are used; however, JIT (Just-In-Time) account creation, where accounts are automatically created and deleted based on IdP allocation, and SCIM directory synchronization are also available. SCIM is only available in the Enterprise edition.

tabs.label: Gemini Enterprise
tabs.body:
Gemini Enterprise is a product that provides internet search, AI assistant, and agent platform capabilities. It includes built-in connectors for business systems such as Confluence, Jira, SharePoint, and ServiceNow, focusing on unifying an organization's documents and work tools into a single search experience.

A Billing Account Administrator role is required to modify subscriptions and licenses. Without this role or the associated permissions, users cannot verify subscriptions, reclaim, or distribute licenses. Remember that management permissions are linked to Google Cloud's billing role.

tabs.label: common structure
tabs.body:
These three products share the same underlying framework, despite differing in names and interfaces. First, they manage members and seats on a workspace basis. Second, they assign access to features and apps based on roles or groups. Third, they integrate with an identity system (IdP) to align with login processes and account lifecycle management.

Therefore, when selecting a product, it is more important to determine how the controls your organization needs are implemented across specific settings in a given interface, rather than focusing solely on the product's name or interface design. The same control may be referred to and located differently across products.

screens.outro: We will continue examining how administrators onboard users and compare the responsibilities associated with API construction.

screens.title: SSO·SCIM, and API Deployment Control Scope
screens.lead: Compare how the responsible party changes by alternately selecting two states. In Business Apps, settings take on the responsibility, while in API development, the team designs it directly.

visual.alt: Comparison between the patterns and API development areas where SSO and SCIM are connected to the product with different roles in the IdP.
labels: SSO: How do you log in?
SCIM: Who owns the account (account creation and deletion synchronization)?

states.label: enterprise apps
states.body:
In enterprise applications, identity and account management are handled through configuration settings. First, it's important to distinguish the roles of SSO and SCIM. SSO defines how users log in, while SCIM manages who has accounts—specifically, it creates and deletes user accounts and groups in alignment with the Identity Provider (IdP). OpenAI documents state that SCIM handles provisioning, while SSO handles authentication methods, and that the two can be independently configured.

Claude categorizes provisioning methods into three types: invite-only (default), JIT (Just-In-Time), and SCIM. SCIM provisions accounts before users log in, based on allocations from the IdP, enabling automated cleanup of former employee accounts. Gemini Enterprise manages subscriptions and licenses through the Billing Account Administrator role. In summary, responsibility for identity, seats, and feature access in enterprise applications lies with the product's provided administrator settings.

states.label: Build your own API
states.body:
If you build services directly using APIs, the administrator console will not automatically follow along. The team must directly design each item themselves. Who can make calls is defined by keys and permission systems, which tools can be used is determined by tool integration design, and what events occurred is recorded directly through custom logs. The management and change history of prompts also fall to the team.

In exchange for this choice, you gain flexibility. Activities such as calling internal systems, performing large-scale processing via automation, or integrating responses into your own screen interfaces and workflows go beyond what can be achieved through app settings alone. While using a platform like the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform—combining construction, scalability, governance, and optimization—can reduce some burdens, the responsibility of determining what and how to control remains with the team.

Therefore, enterprise apps are a suitable choice for rapid deployment, and API development is well-suited for directly designing control and integration.

screens.outro: Having confirmed the difference between the two areas, let's now explain how they are actually divided in real-world scenarios.

screens.title: Explanation: When the legal team's requirements differ from those of the development team
screens.lead: The instructor follows the process of evaluating requirements from both teams. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step. Pay attention to the rationale used for each decision.

visual.alt: A diagram showing the division of legal and development team requirements into app domain and API domain, consolidated into a single responsibility matrix.
labels: Legal Team - Contract summary, external disclosure control, audit possibility
Development team - internal system calls, automated batch processing, proprietary logging

steps.title: Step 1: Write down the legal team's requirements
steps.body: The legal team's requirements are threefold: they want contract summaries generated quickly, they need control over the distribution of contract contents outside the organization, and they require the ability to audit who performed what actions. The starting point is to convert these requirements from human-driven tasks into controlled items that are documented. Summarization corresponds to functionality, control over distribution corresponds to access settings, and auditing corresponds to logging and analysis.

steps.title: Step 2: Verify whether it satisfies the app settings
steps.body: Now verify whether each item is satisfied by enterprise app administrator settings. Members and seats are handled through Workspace Management, feature access through custom roles, and account provisioning via SSO and SCIM. The summary functionality is provided natively by the app, so no additional configuration is needed. Most requirements can be met through existing settings, and building custom solutions is not necessary—because it introduces additional design and operational overhead.

steps.title: Step 3: Record the development team's requirements
steps.body: The development team's requirements are different. It involves calling internal systems, processing large volumes automatically rather than through manual screen interactions, and logging call records in its own proprietary format. All three of these requirements extend beyond the product interface and reach into systems outside the organization.

steps.title: Step 4: Verify the reason why API construction is needed
steps.body: Internal system integration, automated deployment, and built-in logging cannot be achieved solely through app settings. Therefore, the development team chooses to build APIs, taking direct responsibility for key issuance and storage, call permissions, and log design. A key point here is that the control previously obtained through settings in enterprise apps does not automatically transfer to the built environment. In an app, tasks previously handled by the admin console must now be designed and implemented by the team.

steps.title: Step 5: Combine into a single responsibility matrix
steps.body: Finally, we combine the two domains into a single responsibility matrix. Rows represent identity, seat, function access, call permissions, logging, and data export, while columns represent enterprise app and API development. In each cell, we specify who controls what. This matrix forms the foundational structure of corporate standards. When new requirements arise, we first check whether they are satisfied by existing settings, and only move those not satisfied to the development cells for implementation.

screens.outro: I will consolidate the judgment criteria obtained from the case into one screen.

screens.title: Criteria for separating enterprise apps and API construction
screens.lead: I will summarize what I have seen so far into one judgment standard.

paragraphs: Enterprise apps are managed through the functionality provided by the administrator console—specifically workspace management, roles, seats, SSO, and SCIM—for controlling user access and membership. A key strength is the rapid onboarding and pre-existing control capabilities. The three products, while differing in name and interface, share a common structure of managing resources at the workspace level.

Building the API itself involves the team designing aspects such as prompts, tool integration, logging, and permissions. Instead of addressing requirements that cannot be met by the app itself—such as integration with internal systems or automation—the team must directly implement and operate the controls.

SSO and SCIM perform different functions. SSO handles the login process, while SCIM manages account creation and deletion, and can be independently configured. Enabling SSO alone integrates login but may result in leftover accounts for terminated employees.

In practice, departmental requirements are converted into control items and recorded; if they are satisfied through app settings, they are not implemented, and only those not covered by settings are implemented. By combining these two areas into a single responsibility matrix, tools that previously varied by department can now be described under corporate standards.

Finally, let's address a common pitfall. Simply introducing enterprise apps does not automatically eliminate personal account usage. Members must be aware of the tools approved by the organization and their configurations, and the division between which requests are handled via apps and which are handled through built-in features must be clearly shared. A responsibility matrix also serves as a visible document that enforces this agreement. After creating the matrix, whenever a new tool is introduced, it should be compared against the same row to explain department-specific differences within the organization's overall framework. The consolidated matrix should not be treated as a one-time document to be completed and archived; instead, it should be maintained as an ongoing reference that is regularly reviewed as both members and tools evolve.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Enterprise apps choose rapid deployment and API setup as a direct design for control and integration. Requirements satisfied by configuration are not built.

glossary.def: A subscription-based AI service managed through administrator console features such as SSO, SCIM, roles, and workspace settings.
By calling the model API to create a standalone service, the team is responsible for designing authentication, logging, and tool integration.
Members, seats, function access, apps, and analytics are managed by administrators from a single location.
SSO integrates the login method, while SCIM synchronizes the creation and deletion of users and groups with the IdP. Both are configured independently.
An access control method that assigns functional permissions to roles and grants them to members or groups.

misconceptions.myth: Using a business app eliminates the need for separate management.
misconceptions.fact: The app provides management capabilities, but seat assignments, roles, app access, and provisioning methods must be defined by the administrator.

misconceptions.myth: Enabling SSO automatically handles account creation and deletion.
misconceptions.fact: SSO focuses only on the authentication method. Account creation and deletion synchronization falls under SCIM or JIT configurations and is managed separately.

misconceptions.myth: Using an API allows you to directly obtain the management features of enterprise-grade apps.
misconceptions.fact: API is not a management interface but a means of invocation. Controls such as permissions, logging, and tool integration must be designed directly by the team.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Enterprise apps are quickly deployed and controlled using administrator console features.
Building the API itself provides greater flexibility, rather than directly designing control and integration.
SSO handles authentication, while SCIM handles account lifecycle synchronization, and they are independent of each other.
Separate the departmental requirements, then combine them in a responsibility matrix to form the basis of an organization-wide standard.
